result:
Neither, as far as I can tell. The premise that more agents always give better results isn't true, so "five or ten?" isn't the right question yet.

Here's an everyday version. Say you're planning a group project. Two people can split the work and finish sooner. Ten people spend most of their time in meetings, repeating context and fixing mismatched pieces. Agents work the same way. Each agent you add has to be handed the task and the relevant context, usually by reading it again, and that costs tokens (the units models are billed in). It also adds another place for information to get lost or misread when work passes between agents.

For your makerspace assistant, take a request like "How do I set up the laser cutter, and can I book it Thursday?" One agent can handle it: look up the manual page, check the calendar, book the slot. Splitting that into a manual agent, a calendar agent, a booking agent and a coordinator means more model calls for the same answer. That hurts when your sponsor's budget is small.

Splitting usually pays off in two cases:
- **The context gets too big or cluttered for one agent.** For example, the manuals are huge and the noise from searching them drowns out the booking steps.
- **Subtasks are independent and can run in parallel,** such as researching several machines at once.

It usually doesn't pay off when the steps depend on each other, or when a single agent with good tool descriptions can do the job.

So I'd start with one agent and a few well-described tools. Split only when you can name a specific problem the split solves, and measure the cost before and after. "One agent, and here is the failure that would make us add a second" is also an easy position to defend at your design review.

Quick check: in the laser cutter request above, which step would you be most tempted to give its own agent, and what problem would that fix?

I can also teach a lesson on when multi-agent systems pay off. It would fit best after we cover context and memory, which is next on your list.
